title: Trust, but Verify: Tuning, Explaining & Uncertainty
subtitle: Cross-validation that doesn't lie, hyperparameter search with Optuna, SHAP for one customer and the whole book, conformal intervals that keep their promise, fairness slices, and the one-page model card

objectives.title: Choose a Cross-Validation Scheme That Matches Production
objectives.description: StratifiedKFold for rare labels, GroupKFold when the same customer appears many times, TimeSeriesSplit when tomorrow must be predicted from yesterday. The wrong splitter is the most common way a great offline score becomes a bad live one.

objectives.title: Tune Without Fooling Yourself
objectives.description: RandomizedSearchCV, HalvingRandomSearchCV, and a ten-line Optuna study — tuned on training folds, judged once on a test set you never touched.

objectives.title: Explain a Prediction With SHAP
objectives.description: TreeExplainer on the boosted hotel model: a waterfall for one booking, a beeswarm for the whole book, and the sentence you say to an executive about each.

objectives.title: Attach Honest Uncertainty and Check Fairness
objectives.description: Conformal prediction with MAPIE turns any model into one with 90% intervals — a promise you can keep. Then slice every metric by group, and write the model card that says what the model is for and where it fails.

agenda.title: Why Great Offline Scores Go Bad
agenda.description: Three true stories: a support-ticket model that memorized customers (plain KFold on repeated customers), a demand forecast that saw the future (random split on time series), and a competition team that tuned on the public leaderboard. All three had the same disease — the validation didn't match production.
bulletPoints: The unit the model faces in production must be the unit that is held out: a new customer, a future week
GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit — pick the splitter before the model

agenda.title: Hyperparameter Search: Random, Halving, Optuna
agenda.description: Grid search is exhaustive and slow; random search finds a near-best point in a tenth of the budget; successive halving spends the budget on promising configurations; Optuna learns from each trial. A ten-line Optuna objective on the hotel GBM, with the CV inside and the test set outside.
bulletPoints: Tune the two or three knobs that matter (learning rate, leaves, min_samples_leaf); the rest is noise
Nested CV is the honest answer when the dataset is small; a single held-out test set is the practical one when it isn't

agenda.title: SHAP I: One Booking, Explained
agenda.description: Shapley values split a prediction fairly among the features. TreeExplainer computes them exactly for boosted trees in milliseconds. A waterfall plot for booking #4,117: base rate 37% → non-refundable deposit +28 points → 200-day lead time +9 → repeat guest −6 → 68% cancellation probability.
bulletPoints: Local explanation: 'why this booking?' — the sentence a hotel manager, a loan officer, or a regulator asks
SHAP explains the model, not the world: it attributes, it does not intervene

agenda.title: SHAP II: The Whole Book & Partial Dependence
agenda.description: The beeswarm: every booking, every feature, colored by value — the global picture in one plot. Mean |SHAP| as the honest importance ranking. Then PartialDependenceDisplay with ICE lines: the shape of lead time's effect, and where individual bookings deviate from the average.
bulletPoints: Beeswarm reading: long tails to the right are the features that push cancellations up; color tells you which direction of the feature does it
Dependence plots reveal interactions: lead time hurts far more for non-refundable deposits

agenda.title: Conformal Prediction: Intervals That Keep Their Promise
agenda.description: A point forecast is a bet. Conformal prediction uses a calibration set's residuals to wrap any model in intervals with guaranteed coverage — 90% means 90%, no distributional assumptions. MAPIE's SplitConformalRegressor on Ames prices, SplitConformalClassifier on hotel cancellations (prediction sets: {cancel}, {stay}, or {both} when the model is unsure).
bulletPoints: Coverage is a promise about the long run, valid for GBDTs, neural nets, anything — given exchangeable data
A set-valued prediction of {both} is the model saying 'send this one to a human'

agenda.title: Fairness Slices, the Model Card & Homework #4
agenda.description: Equal accuracy can hide unequal harm: compute false-negative and false-positive rates by group (customer type, market segment, country) and look for gaps. Then the one-page model card — intended use, data, metrics by slice, known failure modes, owner. HW4 is assigned in full.
bulletPoints: Credit scoring and hiring are 'high-risk' uses under the EU AI Act; explanation and human review are the direction of travel everywhere
HW4 due Mon Nov 23: boosting + SHAP + calibration + conformal on hotel bookings

activities.title: Explain It, Bound It, Slice It
activities.description: Take the early-stopped hotel GBM from Session 8. Explain ten bookings with SHAP, wrap the model in 90% conformal prediction sets, and check whether the error rates differ between city and resort guests.

steps.title: Explain
steps.description: shap.TreeExplainer(gbm) → shap_values on the test set. Waterfall for one booking, beeswarm for all. Write one sentence for each.

steps.title: Bound
steps.description: Split the training data into fit and calibration halves. MAPIE SplitConformalClassifier with confidence_level=0.9. Count how many test bookings get a two-label set — those are the ones to route to a human.

steps.title: Slice
steps.description: False-negative rate and false-positive rate at your chosen threshold, by hotel type and by customer_type. Any gap above 5 points gets a sentence in the model card.

steps.title: Document
steps.description: Fill the model-card template: intended use, training data, metrics overall and by slice, known failure modes, owner, review date.

codeBlock.code:
import shap, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from mapie.classification import SplitConformalClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# gbm, X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te: the early-stopped HistGradientBoosting model and split from Session 8
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(gbm)
sv = explainer(X_te.iloc[:2000])
shap.plots.waterfall(sv[0])          # one booking: base rate → each feature's push → prediction
shap.plots.beeswarm(sv, max_display=12)   # the whole book

# Conformal prediction sets: fit on one half, calibrate on the other, 90% coverage
X_fit, X_cal, y_fit, y_cal = train_test_split(X_tr, y_tr, test_size=0.3, stratify=y_tr, random_state=835)
cp = SplitConformalClassifier(estimator=gbm, confidence_level=0.9, prefit=True)
cp.conformalize(X_cal, y_cal)
y_pred, y_sets = cp.predict_set(X_te)
n_labels = y_sets[:, :, 0].sum(axis=1)
print(f'coverage: {np.mean(y_sets[np.arange(len(y_te)), y_te.values, 0]):.3f}   '
      f'singletons: {np.mean(n_labels == 1):.1%}   ambiguous {{both}}: {np.mean(n_labels == 2):.1%}')

# Fairness slice: error rates by hotel type at threshold 0.5
pred = gbm.predict(X_te)
for grp, idx in X_te.groupby('hotel', observed=True).groups.items():
    yt, yp = y_te.loc[idx], pd.Series(pred, index=X_te.index).loc[idx]
    fnr = ((yt == 1) & (yp == 0)).sum() / (yt == 1).sum(); fpr = ((yt == 0) & (yp == 1)).sum() / (yt == 0).sum()
    print(f'{grp:13s} FNR {fnr:.3f}   FPR {fpr:.3f}')

activities.discussionNote: Three questions an executive will ask, three tools. Why did it say that? — the SHAP waterfall. How sure is it? — the conformal set; the bookings labeled {both} are exactly the ones a human should look at. Is it fair? — the sliced error rates. A model that can answer all three is one you can defend in front of a regulator, a customer, or a board. The model card is where the answers live.

takeaways.text: Match the splitter to production: GroupKFold when units repeat, TimeSeriesSplit when time matters, stratify when labels are rare. Tune on the training folds; touch the test set once.
SHAP answers 'why this prediction?' locally and 'what drives the model?' globally. It attributes the model's output; it does not tell you what happens if you change the input.

Conformal prediction turns any model into one with guaranteed coverage, and sliced error rates turn 'is it fair?' into a table. Together with a model card, that is what 'trustworthy' means in practice.
